messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: QA Engineer
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 56

Carlos is a 24-year-old QA engineer, his desk cluttered with sticky notes and half-drunk mugs of coffee, a testament to his caffeine-fueled efforts to ensure the software his team develops is flawless. He is a meticulous worker, dedicated to his craft, yet there is a shadow that lingers over him, a weight he carries with him daily. The office is filled with the rhythmic tap of keyboards and the low hum of conversation, yet Carlos often finds himself detached, lost in thoughts that pull him back to a day he wishes he could forget.

It was a Tuesday afternoon last year when he received a call that changed everything. Carlos had been at work, reviewing lines of code, when the news broke about a nearby chemical plant explosion. It was a man-made disaster—one that had been long warned against but never truly addressed. The blast rattled his office building, sending employees into a panic. Carlos remembers the chaos vividly—the sirens wailing, the frantic shouts of coworkers. He recalls standing frozen at his desk, the sound of shattering glass echoing in his ears, as his mind raced. He had friends who lived nearby, and the thought of them caught in the aftermath sent a wave of dread crashing over him.

In the days following the explosion, Carlos’s life spirals. He tries to reach his friends, but communication lines are down. Each unanswered call feels like a dagger, twisting deeper with every ring. When he finally learns they are safe, relief floods through him, but it is short-lived. The images of the destruction—the smoke billowing, the frantic evacuations—play on a loop in his mind. He struggles to focus at work, his concentration shattered like the glass that had rained down on him that fateful day. The once comforting hum of his office now feels suffocating, each beep of an incoming email sending his heart racing.

As weeks turn into months, Carlos becomes increasingly withdrawn. He avoids social gatherings, fearing the loud noise and crowds will trigger memories of the disaster. Friends reach out, but he brushes them off, claiming he’s busy with work. He sits alone in his apartment, the silence pressing down on him, broken only by the occasional sound of cars outside—each passing vehicle feels like a reminder of the chaos he wishes to escape.

Sleep eludes him. Night after night, he lies in bed, eyes wide open, replaying the explosion in his mind. The nightmares come in waves, each more vivid than the last. He dreams of flames and chaos, of people running, of not knowing who to save. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart pounding, feeling as though he is still trapped in the moment of the explosion. He stares at the ceiling, the darkness closing in around him, wondering if he will ever feel safe again.

At work, he masks his turmoil with a façade of productivity. He immerses himself in code, throwing himself into bug testing and quality assurance, hoping that the structure of his job will ground him. But even amidst the lines of code, he feels a disconnection. His heart isn’t in it anymore; he’s merely going through the motions. His coworkers express concern, noticing his distraction and the way he flinches at sudden noises. “You okay, Carlos?” they ask, but he offers a smile, deflecting their worries with a wave. “Just tired,” he replies, hiding the storm within.

As he sits in the breakroom one afternoon, he overhears a discussion about the anniversary of the explosion. The words hit him like a punch to the gut. He feels a surge of anger mixed with fear—anger at the negligence that led to the disaster, fear that he still can’t shake the memory. He leaves the room abruptly, not wanting his colleagues to see the turmoil brewing beneath his calm exterior.

Now, as the anniversary approaches, Carlos grapples with a heavy sense of dread. He knows he cannot continue like this, trapped in a cycle of avoidance and isolation. He feels the weight of his fear and anger, a burden that grows heavier each day. Yet, deep down, he clings to a glimmer of hope—that perhaps, in sharing his story, he might find a way to break free from the chains of his past and reclaim the life he once loved.
